economic_impact.body: Information-processing investment growth increased materially to 20.6%. Nonfarm-business productivity grew 2.2% as real output rose 2.5%, while real hourly compensation increased 0.6%. Investment is expanding much faster than the broad outcome measures, but that contrast does not measure AI’s return: the aggregate series cannot isolate AI’s contribution to output, productivity, or pay.
economic_impact.headline: Information-processing investment accelerates while broad outcomes move more slowly

finance.body: Borrower strain rose materially to 30.0, while lender strain edged up to 18.9. Operating cash flow still covers current CapEx at 1.24 times, but the margin has narrowed, and forward commitments remain substantial at 4.13 times current CapEx. CNBC reported that Moody’s sees private credit holding firm despite the AI debt wave. Credit therefore remains available in aggregate, but the rising strain measures and large commitment load leave future financing important.
finance.headline: Borrower strain rises while current CapEx remains internally covered

grid_storage.body: Electric-power construction growth accelerated materially to 14.0%. At the same time, the active interconnection queue totals 2,061 GW, including 552.7 GW of storage, and only 24.2% of queued capacity has reached executed-agreement or construction stages. Current infrastructure work is expanding quickly, but most proposed generation and storage capacity remains at earlier stages of development.
grid_storage.headline: Power construction accelerates, but most queued capacity remains at earlier stages

macro.body: The physical layer remains the clearest source of momentum. Electric-power construction growth accelerated materially to 14.0%, semiconductor and electronic-component output grew 19.9%, and available records show 1,556 data-center sites in development against 3,068 operating sites. The electricity pipeline is large but immature: only 24.2% of the 2,061 GW active interconnection queue has reached executed-agreement or construction stages, although storage alone accounts for 552.7 GW. Active construction and a large inventory of proposed capacity therefore coexist with substantial execution still ahead. Financial support has softened rather than disappeared. The AI Equity Index slipped to 34.7, while the median one-year return fell materially to 7.8%; 58.3% of covered companies remain positive over one year. Borrower strain rose materially to 30.0, even as operating cash flow continued to cover current CapEx at 1.24 times and forward commitments stood at 4.13 times current CapEx. Recent reports capture the tension: the Financial Times said technology shares fell as earnings fueled concern about AI spending, while CNBC reported Moody’s view that private credit remains firm despite the AI debt wave. Downstream transmission remains less broad. Businesses reporting current AI use account for 24.6%, compared with 28.6% expecting to use it within six months. Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth, and it is power and communication construction, at 0.8%. Business deployment continues to trail near-term intentions, while the clearest labor gain remains tied to building the physical infrastructure.
macro.headline: Physical investment strengthens as market returns narrow and financing strain rises

market.body: The AI Equity Index edged down to 34.7, and 58.3% of covered companies have positive one-year returns. The median one-year return fell more sharply to 7.8%. A majority of companies remains positive, but the typical gain has narrowed. The Financial Times reported that U.S. technology stocks fell after earnings renewed concerns about AI spending, showing greater investor scrutiny without establishing a reversal in the investment cycle.
market.headline: Market gains narrow as spending concerns return after earnings

power.body: Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.5%, nearly twice the 1.8% increase in total retail demand, while retail electricity prices are up 5.1%. Net planned generation additions total 227.6 GW, but they remain pipeline capacity rather than operating supply. Utility Dive reported on Google’s virtual power plant in PJM in the context of intensifying competition for electricity. The project adds a nontraditional response to the power challenge, although the reported development does not show its scale or whether it can materially ease supply pressure. The figures also do not establish AI as the cause of broader demand or price growth.
power.headline: Google’s PJM virtual power plant adds another response as electricity demand and prices rise

workforce.body: Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel shows positive employment growth: power and communication construction, at 0.8%. Two channels have positive real-earnings growth, so earnings growth is somewhat broader than headcount growth. CNBC separately reported that some companies are rehiring workers after deciding they moved too quickly with AI-driven layoffs. That report complicates a simple displacement narrative, but the measured employment gains remain narrow and concentrated in physical infrastructure.
workforce.headline: AI-linked employment growth remains confined to physical infrastructure

editorial_briefing.style_reference: AI Macro is a research platform that examines the development of the U.S. AI economy from capital investment and physical construction through deployment, adoption, and economic results. It uses publicly available data to relate corporate and market activity to the physical systems required to support the buildout. It evaluates the extent to which that investment produces durable economic value and how its effects are transmitted through the broader U.S. economy.

body.text: The share of covered companies with positive one-year returns rose materially to 60.8%, and the median one-year return increased to 12.6%. The AI Equity Index only edged up to 35.5, so the improvement is more visible in breadth and the typical return than in the headline index. Recent company reports remain mixed. CNBC reported that Microsoft shares rose 4% after cloud growth drove an earnings and revenue beat, while Reuters highlighted Anthropic’s soaring sales and steep losses as a test for a potential IPO.

body.text: The definition-matched debt-financing pulse increased slightly to 0.5, and lender strain also edged up, to 20.1. The Chicago Fed’s NFCI remains negative at -0.46, but its 0.07 rise over three months was material, consistent with somewhat firmer financial conditions. Bloomberg reported that Oracle is offering $10 billion of high-grade dollar bonds, while Reuters reported concern that AI-related debt could pressure European bond markets. The developments show issuance continuing alongside concern about how markets absorb additional debt; they do not establish a broad credit disruption.

headline.text: Debt activity and lender strain edge higher

body.text: Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.5%, versus 1.8% for total retail demand, while retail electricity prices are up 5.1%. Utility Dive reported that PSEG Power plans a 200 MW nuclear uprate as it considers data-center deals. The reported uprate gives a defined project and scale, although it remains planned. Across the broader pipeline horizon, net planned generation additions total 227.6 GW. The PSEG report ties one proposed project to potential data-center business; the aggregate demand and price figures do not isolate AI’s role.

Market gains broaden amid firmer financing signals and an immature power pipeline

paragraphs.text: The clearest near-term change is the broader market advance. Positive one-year returns now cover 60.8% of tracked companies, and the median return has increased materially to 12.6%, while the AI Equity Index only edged up to 35.5. The improvement therefore extends through more covered stocks rather than reflecting a sharp move in the headline index. CNBC’s report that Microsoft shares rose 4% after cloud growth drove an earnings and revenue beat provides one company-level example, not proof of a sector-wide earnings acceleration.

Financing remains active, but the indicators have become somewhat firmer. The debt-financing pulse and lender strain both edged higher, and the NFCI rose materially over three months even though it remains negative. Bloomberg reported Oracle’s $10 billion high-grade bond offering; Reuters separately reported concern that AI-related debt could pressure European bond markets. The reports show issuance coming to market alongside greater attention to debt absorption, but they do not establish a broad credit break.

Power remains an execution challenge as much as a planning problem. Commercial electricity demand is growing faster than total retail demand, and net planned generation additions total 227.6 GW. Separately, the active interconnection queue stands at 2,061 GW, but only 24.2% has reached executed-agreement or construction stages, and 13% of the 2000–2020 cohort reached operation. Utility Dive’s report of PSEG’s planned 200 MW nuclear uprate shows one defined response tied to prospective data-center deals, but it does not erase the distinction between proposed and operating supply.

Broader economic transmission remains less clear. Businesses reporting current AI use account for 24.6%, versus 28.6% expecting use within six months. Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth: power and communication construction, at 0.8%. Nonfarm-business productivity is growing 2.2%, but that aggregate measure cannot identify AI’s contribution. The evidence is therefore more specific about ongoing adoption and infrastructure employment than about broad AI-attributable economic gains.

macro.analysis: The clearest near-term change is the broader market advance. Positive one-year returns now cover 60.8% of tracked companies, and the median return has increased materially to 12.6%, while the AI Equity Index only edged up to 35.5. The improvement therefore extends through more covered stocks rather than reflecting a sharp move in the headline index. CNBC’s report that Microsoft shares rose 4% after cloud growth drove an earnings and revenue beat provides one company-level example, not proof of a sector-wide earnings acceleration. Financing remains active, but the indicators have become somewhat firmer. The debt-financing pulse and lender strain both edged higher, and the NFCI rose materially over three months even though it remains negative. Bloomberg reported Oracle’s $10 billion high-grade bond offering; Reuters separately reported concern that AI-related debt could pressure European bond markets. Separately, the active interconnection queue stands at 2,061 GW, but only 24.2% has reached executed-agreement or construction stages, and 13% of the 2000–2020 cohort reached operation. Utility Dive’s report of PSEG’s planned 200 MW nuclear uprate shows one defined response tied to prospective data-center deals, but it does not erase the distinction between proposed and operating supply. Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth: power and communication construction, at 0.8%. Nonfarm-business productivity is growing 2.2%, but that aggregate measure cannot identify AI’s contribution. The evidence is therefore more specific about ongoing adoption and infrastructure employment than about broad AI-attributable economic gains.
